_README: TEMPLATE for IT/platform teams. Deploy to /Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/managed-settings.json (macOS), /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (Linux and WSL), or C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json (Windows). Claude Code does not read the legacy Windows path C:\ProgramData\ClaudeCode\managed-settings.json, so a file left there enforces nothing. This file CANNOT be overridden by any user or project configuration. Read docs/org-policy.md BEFORE deploying — layer 5 is the layer teams reach for last and misuse first, and the misuse is worse than the gap.
_PRINCIPLE: Enforce the intolerable, permit the rest. These controls protect against the ENGINEER's mistake, not the agent's — they are the rules that must hold regardless of what any individual configures. Everything merely serious belongs in the project's own .claude/settings.json where teams can adapt it. An org policy that treats every engineer as an adversary loses them to shadow tooling, which has NO layers at all.
_1_FORCED_AUTHENTICATION: So nobody runs against production with personal credentials.
_2_NO_BYPASS: disableBypassPermissionsMode makes the permission layer non-optional. allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly stays FALSE deliberately: this deny list is a FLOOR, not a ceiling — projects must stay free to add their own rules. Setting it true is maximalism, and maximalism is how teams end up outside the governed environment.
_3_THE_NON_OVERRIDABLE_SECURITY_FLOOR: This is the org-scale answer to the plugin trap. A plugin CANNOT ship `permissions`, so every consuming project must copy the deny floor by hand — and the SessionStart sentinel exists only to catch the ones that didn't. Deployed here, the floor simply EXISTS everywhere and no local override can weaken it: no copying, no drift, and the sentinel reports it complete. Keep this list to the CATASTROPHIC tier only — secrets, privilege escalation, remote code execution, irreversible infrastructure. The plugin's fuller floor (build-artifact Read denies etc.) is a context-economy concern, NOT a security one, and belongs in project settings rather than non-overridable org policy; so does Read(**/*secret*), a broad name glob that the sentinel does not require from a managed floor carrying this list.
_3a_POWERSHELL_MIRRORS: Every shell deny has a PowerShell(...) mirror. The PowerShell tool is on by default on Windows (with or without Git Bash, for claude.ai and Console accounts), and a Bash(...) rule never matches it. Claude Code checks each stage of a PowerShell pipeline on its own, so `irm <url> | iex` is denied at Invoke-Expression itself (aliases such as iex match the cmdlet rule). Drive roots are written as / and C:/ because a backslash in a rule can be read as an escape character; the sdh dangerous-command-blocker hook covers the C: backslash form.
_4_MCP_SUPPLY_CHAIN: Restricting which MCP servers may be connected is a supply-chain control at org scale — server vetting made mandatory rather than advisory. An MCP tool description is a prompt the model obeys, so an unvetted server is an unvetted instruction source. Replace the examples with your actual vetted servers.

deniedMcpServers._comment: Default-deny: anything not explicitly allowed above

_5_REQUIRE_THE_AUDIT_TRAIL: The audit trail is the artifact you reconstruct an incident from, so it must not be optional. Enabling the sdh plugin org-wide keeps audit-logger.py registered on every session; it announces any gap rather than failing silently. Pin a version rather than tracking a moving target.
companyAnnouncements: Security standards: the `std-security` skill loads automatically on any source file you edit.
Vague requirement? Run /sdh:requirements-consultant before writing code.

A `GOVERNANCE GAP` message at session start means the permission deny floor is missing, or incomplete, across every settings source the plugin can read (project, local, user, and a file-based managed settings file) — fix it before doing sensitive work.
